props.title: Adam's Rib

sections.content: Adam's Rib (1949) stands as one of Hollywood's sharpest battle-of-the-sexes comedies, featuring the incomparable pairing of Spencer Tracy and Katharine Hepburn in their sixth collaboration. As married lawyers arguing opposite sides of an attempted murder case, they bring the courtroom drama home in ways that challenged 1940s gender politics. Director George Cukor, known for drawing exceptional performances from actresses like in The Philadelphia Story (1940), crafts perfect timing between the leads while tackling serious themes about equality and justice through wit rather than preaching.

sections.content: The Tracy-Hepburn dynamic defined sophisticated romantic comedy for a generation. Their nine films together, starting with Woman of the Year (1942), created a template for intelligent couples sparring that influenced everything from His Girl Friday (1940) to When Harry Met Sally (1989). In Adam's Rib, their natural chemistry elevates Ruth Gordon and Garson Kanin's razor-sharp screenplay beyond mere courtroom drama into a thoughtful examination of marriage, equality, and justice.

Director George Cukor's masterstroke was treating serious feminist themes with a light touch. Unlike heavier social issue films of the era like Gentleman's Agreement (1947), Adam's Rib makes its points through humor and charm. The film's influence can be seen in later legal comedies like Legally Blonde (2001), which similarly uses wit to challenge gender assumptions in the courtroom. SUBHEAD: Gender Politics in Golden Age Hollywood

sections.content: While many 1940s films reinforced traditional gender roles, Adam's Rib dared to present a professional woman as equal to her male counterpart. Hepburn's Amanda Bonner argues forcefully for a woman's right to equal justice, while never losing her humanity or humor. This approach distinguished it from both the submissive female characters common in the era and the more strident message films that would follow in the 1950s and 60s.
